title: GLP-1 Medicines — How Ozempic, Wegovy & Mounjaro Work
tagline: The gut hormone behind the biggest shift in medicine in a generation — how it works, the newest drugs, the muscle question, and the honest risks.
description: A plain-language, up-to-date (2026) tour of the GLP-1 revolution: the incretin biology, how the drugs were engineered, the newest dual/triple agonists and the first oral pill, what the trials really showed, a special section on muscle loss and how the newest drugs preserve it, and an honest account of the serious side effects. Educational only — not medical advice.

intro.hook: A hormone from your gut, first noticed in a lizard's venom, turned out to be a weight and diabetes drug.
body: For decades there was an unexplained observation: glucose taken by mouth triggers far more insulin than the same glucose injected into a vein. The body clearly knew the difference between eating and being dosed. Something in the gut was signalling ahead.

That something was GLP-1, and it does several things at once — amplifies insulin only when glucose is high, slows stomach emptying, and reduces appetite through the brain. The natural hormone is destroyed within minutes, which is why the drugs are chemically modified to survive for a week.
This course explains the mechanism honestly: what these medicines do, what they cost physiologically, why the weight returns when they stop, and which claims about them are ahead of the evidence.

why.title: The glucose gate matters
why.text: GLP-1 amplifies insulin only when blood sugar is already high — which is why it rarely causes hypoglycaemia alone.

why.title: Appetite is physiological
why.text: These drugs work on the signalling that governs hunger, which reframes a condition long treated as a failure of character.

why.title: Honest limitations
why.text: Muscle loss, gastrointestinal effects, cost, and regain after stopping are part of the real picture.

intro.closer: The stabilising trick came from exendin-4, in the saliva of the Gila monster. It lasts hours where the human hormone lasts minutes.

concepts.title: The Incretin Effect — your gut talks to your pancreas
concepts.summary: After you eat, your intestine releases hormones that tell the pancreas to make insulin — before blood sugar even climbs. GLP-1 is the star of that system.

cards.h: Eat a meal, and your gut sends a chemical telegram
cards.md:
Swallow some food and cells lining your intestine start releasing hormones into the blood. These are the **incretins** — chemical telegrams that say *"food is coming, get ready."* The most important one is **GLP-1** (glucagon-like peptide-1), released by **L-cells** in the lower gut, with a partner called **GIP** from the upper gut.

Every GLP-1 medicine — Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and the rest — is a copy of this natural *"food is coming"* signal, turned up and made to last.

cards.h: The proof: sugar by mouth beats sugar by vein
cards.md:
Here's the classic experiment. Give someone glucose **by mouth**, then on another day give the exact same rise in blood sugar **through a vein**. The mouthful triggers *far more insulin* — even though the blood sugar is identical.

Why? The vein bypasses the gut, so no incretin telegram is sent. That extra insulin from eating — up to **half to two-thirds** of your after-meal insulin — is the **incretin effect**. In type 2 diabetes this effect is blunted, which is part of why the drugs that restore it work so well.

questions.prompt: What are incretins?
options: Gut hormones released after eating that prime the pancreas to make insulin
Enzymes in the stomach that digest fat
A type of insulin made in the liver
feedback: Correct — GLP-1 and GIP are the incretins, released by the gut when food arrives.
No — incretins are signalling hormones, not digestive enzymes.
No — incretins are hormones, not sugars.
No — insulin comes from the pancreas; incretins are separate gut hormones that trigger it.

questions.prompt: The same rise in blood sugar produces MORE insulin when glucose is taken by mouth than by vein. Why?
options: The mouth route lets the gut release incretins, which add an extra insulin push
Vein glucose is destroyed before it reaches the pancreas
The stomach makes its own insulin
feedback: Correct — that extra push is the incretin effect; the vein bypasses the gut signal.
No — it's a hormonal signal from the gut, not a physical squeeze.
No — vein glucose raises blood sugar the same amount; the difference is the missing gut signal.
No — the stomach doesn't make insulin.

questions.prompt: Which cells release GLP-1?
feedback: Correct — intestinal L-cells release GLP-1 in response to nutrients.
No — red blood cells carry oxygen, not GLP-1.
No — the liver responds to insulin but doesn't release GLP-1.
No — while GLP-1 also acts in the brain, it's released by gut L-cells.

concepts.title: Four Jobs GLP-1 Does
concepts.summary: GLP-1 lowers blood sugar and appetite through four coordinated actions — and one clever detail keeps it from causing dangerous lows.

cards.h: Insulin up, glucagon down — but only when sugar is high
cards.md:
GLP-1's first two jobs are on the pancreas:

- **Turns insulin UP** in the beta-cells (insulin clears sugar from the blood).
- **Turns glucagon DOWN** in the alpha-cells (glucagon is insulin's opposite — it *raises* sugar).

The crucial detail: this happens **only when blood sugar is elevated** — it's *glucose-dependent*. When your sugar is normal, GLP-1 goes quiet. That's why GLP-1 drugs alone rarely cause **hypoglycemia** (dangerous low blood sugar) — a big safety advantage over older diabetes drugs.

cards.h: Slow the stomach, quiet the appetite
cards.md:
The other two jobs explain the weight loss:

- **Slows gastric emptying** — food leaves your stomach more slowly, so you feel full longer and blood sugar rises more gently after meals.
- **Acts on the brain** — GLP-1 reaches the **hypothalamus**, the appetite control centre, and dials down hunger and food-seeking.

Eat less, feel full sooner, absorb sugar more smoothly. The same slowed stomach that curbs appetite is also behind the most common side effect — nausea.

questions.prompt: Why do GLP-1 drugs rarely cause dangerously low blood sugar on their own?
options: Their insulin-boosting action is glucose-dependent — it switches off when sugar is normal
They contain sugar to top you up
They stop the pancreas from ever making insulin
They only work in the brain
feedback: Correct — glucose-dependence means no extra insulin push when sugar is already normal.
No — they don't contain sugar.
No — they boost insulin (when needed), not block it.
No — they act on the pancreas and gut too; the safety comes from glucose-dependence.

questions.prompt: Which action most directly explains the appetite reduction?
options: Action on the hypothalamus (brain appetite centre) plus slowed stomach emptying
feedback: Correct — brain appetite signalling plus a slower stomach make you eat less.
No — GLP-1 lowers glucagon.
No — it slows, not speeds, the stomach.
No — it boosts insulin when needed.

questions.prompt: The most common side effect (nausea) comes from which action?
feedback: Correct — the same slowed stomach that curbs appetite can cause nausea.
No — glucagon suppression affects blood sugar, not nausea.
No — insulin affects blood sugar.
No — appetite signalling reduces hunger; nausea is the stomach-slowing effect.

concepts.title: The Two-Minute Problem — why you can't just inject GLP-1
concepts.summary: Natural GLP-1 is destroyed within about two minutes. Turning it into a once-a-week medicine was a feat of protein engineering.

cards.h: An enzyme chops it up almost instantly
cards.md:
Here's the obstacle drug companies had to beat: **natural GLP-1 lasts only about 1–2 minutes** in the blood. An enzyme called **DPP-4** (dipeptidyl peptidase-4) snips off its end almost as fast as the gut makes it.

So you can't bottle GLP-1 and inject it — it would be gone before it did anything. The whole drug industry around these medicines is really the story of *making GLP-1 survive*.

cards.h: Two engineering tricks: dodge the enzyme, grab a taxi
cards.md:
The medicines beat the two-minute problem with two changes to the molecule:

1. **Resist the enzyme** — tweak the spot DPP-4 attacks so it can't cut.
2. **Hitch a ride on albumin** — attach a **fatty-acid tail** that clings to *albumin*, the most abundant protein in blood. Albumin acts like a slow taxi, releasing the drug gradually over days.

Together these stretch GLP-1's life from **minutes to a week** — which is why one injection now lasts seven days. (A related class, the *gliptins*, instead blocks DPP-4 to protect your own GLP-1 — milder, older diabetes pills.)

questions.prompt: Why can't natural GLP-1 be used directly as a medicine?
options: The enzyme DPP-4 destroys it within about two minutes
The stomach digests it into sugar
feedback: Correct — DPP-4 degrades native GLP-1 in ~1–2 minutes.
No — size isn't the barrier; its short lifespan is.
No — the problem is rapid enzymatic breakdown, not allergy.
No — it's degraded by DPP-4 in the blood, not digested to sugar.

questions.prompt: How does a fatty-acid tail make semaglutide last a week?
options: It binds albumin in the blood, which slowly releases the drug over days
It makes the drug heavier so it sinks
It turns the drug into fat
It lets the drug be swallowed
feedback: Correct — albumin acts as a slow-release reservoir.
No — it's about albumin binding, not weight.
No — the drug still acts on GLP-1 receptors; it isn't converted to fat.
No — the tail extends half-life; oral versions need separate tricks.

questions.prompt: What does the enzyme DPP-4 do to GLP-1?
options: Cuts it, inactivating it within minutes
feedback: Correct — DPP-4 cleaves and inactivates GLP-1 rapidly.
No — DPP-4 breaks it down, not builds it.
No — DPP-4 degrades it; it doesn't transport it.
No — GLP-1 triggers insulin but isn't converted into it.

concepts.title: The Drug Family — a plain-language field guide
concepts.summary: The confusing brand names map onto just a handful of molecules. Here's who's who as of 2026.

cards.md:
The brand names multiply because the *same molecule* gets a different name for diabetes vs weight loss. The key players:

- **Semaglutide** = **Ozempic** (diabetes, weekly shot), **Wegovy** (obesity, weekly shot), **Rybelsus** (a daily pill). The workhorse single GLP-1.
- **Tirzepatide** = **Mounjaro** (diabetes), **Zepbound** (obesity). A **dual** agonist — GLP-1 *plus* GIP (next lesson).
- **Liraglutide** (Victoza / Saxenda) — an older *daily* shot.
- **Dulaglutide** (Trulicity) — weekly, diabetes.
- **Exenatide** — the original, derived from **Gila monster** venom (its natural GLP-1 look-alike resists the DPP-4 enzyme).

cards.h: 2026's headline: the first GLP-1 you can just swallow
cards.md:
The big 2026 change is a **pill that finally works like the shots**. **Orforglipron** (brand **Foundayo**) was FDA-approved in **April 2026** — the first **oral small-molecule** GLP-1.

What makes it different from the older Rybelsus pill: orforglipron is *not* a fragile peptide, so there's **no fasting or water ritual** — you just take it. In its ATTAIN-1 trial it produced about **11–12% weight loss** at ~17 months. A daily pill with no needle is expected to widen access enormously.

*(This lesson is educational, not medical advice — drug choice is a decision for you and your clinician.)*

questions.prompt: Ozempic and Wegovy contain the same active drug. What is it?
feedback: Correct — both are semaglutide; Ozempic is branded for diabetes, Wegovy for obesity.
No — tirzepatide is Mounjaro/Zepbound.
No — metformin is a different, older diabetes drug.
No — semaglutide mimics GLP-1; it isn't insulin.

questions.prompt: What was notable about orforglipron (Foundayo), approved in 2026?
options: It's the first oral small-molecule GLP-1 — a pill with no fasting ritual
feedback: Correct — the first non-peptide oral GLP-1, taken like an ordinary pill.
No — injectable GLP-1s existed for years.
No — it's a single GLP-1 agonist, not a triple.
No — it treats type 2 diabetes/obesity, and cures nothing.

questions.prompt: The original drug in this class, exenatide, was derived from what?
options: A GLP-1 look-alike in Gila monster venom
feedback: Correct — exendin-4 from the Gila monster naturally resists DPP-4.
No — it's a GLP-1 mimic, not insulin.
No — it's a peptide from lizard venom.
No — that was the source of early insulin, not exenatide.

concepts.title: Why 'Dual' and 'Triple' Agonists Hit Harder
concepts.summary: Adding more gut-hormone signals to GLP-1 pushes weight loss from ~15% toward ~30%.

cards.h: Tirzepatide: GLP-1 plus a second hormone (GIP)
cards.md:
If one incretin helps, why not two? **Tirzepatide** (Mounjaro / Zepbound) activates **both GLP-1 and GIP** receptors — a **dual agonist**. GIP adds its own effects on insulin, appetite and fat handling.

The payoff is real: head-to-head against semaglutide (the SURMOUNT-5 trial), tirzepatide delivered about **20% weight loss versus 14%**. Two signals beat one.

cards.h: Retatrutide: a triple, adding a 'burn more' signal
cards.md:
The next step adds a *third* receptor. **Retatrutide** is a **triple agonist** — GLP-1 + GIP + **glucagon**. That last one sounds backwards (glucagon *raises* blood sugar), but at these doses it also **boosts energy expenditure and fat burning** in the liver, while GLP-1 keeps appetite and sugar in check.

In its Phase 3 TRIUMPH trials (2026) retatrutide reached up to about **30% weight loss** — approaching what bariatric surgery achieves. It's not yet approved (filing expected around 2027). Note: a different combo, **CagriSema**, *missed* its head-to-head goal against tirzepatide — more targets isn't automatically better; the biology has to work.

questions.prompt: What makes tirzepatide a 'dual' agonist?
options: It activates both the GLP-1 and GIP receptors
feedback: Correct — GLP-1 + GIP, two incretin receptors.
No — 'dual' refers to two hormone targets, not dosing.
No — it's a single injection.
No — 'dual' means two receptor targets.

questions.prompt: Retatrutide adds a third target, glucagon. Why help a hormone that RAISES blood sugar?
options: At these doses glucagon signalling boosts energy expenditure and fat burning, while GLP-1 controls appetite and sugar
It has no effect and is just marketing
feedback: Correct — the glucagon arm drives fat oxidation/energy use; GLP-1 offsets its sugar effect.
No — the arms are balanced deliberately, not cancelled.
No — cost isn't the rationale.
No — it meaningfully increases weight loss in trials.

questions.prompt: In the SURMOUNT-5 head-to-head, tirzepatide vs semaglutide gave roughly:
feedback: Correct — about 20.2% vs 13.7%.
No — the losses were larger than that.
No — those figures are far too high.
No — tirzepatide was clearly superior.

concepts.title: What the Trials Actually Showed
concepts.summary: Beyond weight: these drugs now have hard evidence for heart and kidney protection — not just the scale.

cards.md:
Roughly, average weight loss in the big trials:

- **Semaglutide (Wegovy)** — about **15%** (STEP program).
- **Tirzepatide (Zepbound)** — about **20–22%** (SURMOUNT).
- **Orforglipron pill** — about **11–12%** (ATTAIN-1, 2026).
- **Retatrutide (triple, not yet approved)** — up to about **30%** (TRIUMPH, 2026).

For comparison, lifestyle changes alone average ~5%. These are the first medicines to rival surgery.

cards.h: The bigger deal: hearts and kidneys
cards.md:
Weight is the headline, but the practice-changing result is **organ protection**. In the **SELECT** trial, semaglutide cut **heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular death by ~20%** in people with obesity and heart disease *who did not have diabetes* — the first time a weight-loss drug proved it protects the heart.

Other trials show **kidney protection** (FLOW) and benefit in a form of **heart failure** (HFpEF). The message: these are metabolic medicines that happen to cause weight loss — not merely cosmetic.

questions.prompt: What did the SELECT trial prove for semaglutide?
options: It cut heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular death (~20%) in people with obesity and heart disease, without diabetes
It only worked in people with diabetes
It had no effect on the heart
feedback: Correct — the first cardiovascular-outcome win for an obesity drug.
No — it doesn't address type 1 diabetes.
No — the SELECT population specifically did NOT have diabetes.
No — it reduced cardiovascular events.

questions.prompt: Ranked by average trial weight loss, which is highest?
feedback: Correct — the triple agonist retatrutide led at ~30% in TRIUMPH.
No — semaglutide is ~15%.
No — the pill is ~11%.
No — lifestyle alone averages ~5%.

questions.prompt: Why do doctors call these 'metabolic' rather than merely 'weight-loss' drugs?
options: They also protect the heart and kidneys, independent of the weight lost
feedback: Correct — organ-protective effects go beyond the scale.
No — no caffeine involved.
No — the point is they do far more than change appearance.
No — they reduce appetite via hormone signalling, not forced starvation.

concepts.title: ★ Where the Lost Weight Comes From — the muscle problem
concepts.summary: Not all weight is fat. A large slice of the weight lost on these drugs is muscle — and that matters for strength, metabolism and healthy ageing.

cards.h: A quarter to a third of the loss is muscle
cards.md:
Step on a scale and it shows one number — but your body is really **fat mass** plus **lean mass** (muscle, organs, bone, water). When you lose weight *any* way, some of both goes.

The catch with GLP-1 drugs: because the weight comes off fast and appetite drops, studies find that **roughly 15–45% of the weight lost is lean tissue — mostly muscle** (commonly cited as about a quarter to a third). The animation shows this: the body-mass column shrinks, but look at *what* you lost.

cards.h: Why muscle loss is more than a vanity issue
cards.md:
Muscle isn't just for looks. It's your **metabolic engine** (it burns calories and soaks up blood sugar), your **strength and balance** (preventing falls), and a **reserve** you draw on when ill.

Losing muscle matters most for two groups: **older adults** — who are already losing muscle to age (*sarcopenia*) and can least afford more — and anyone who **stops the drug** and regains weight as *fat*, ending up with a worse fat-to-muscle ratio than they started. This is why 'quality of weight loss', not just quantity, is the new frontier — and why the next lesson matters.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much of the weight lost on a standard GLP-1 is lean tissue (mostly muscle)?
options: About a quarter to a third (15–45% in studies)
feedback: Correct — commonly about 25–33%, with a studied range of ~15–45%.
No — a substantial fraction is lean tissue, not fat.
No — that would be catastrophic; the figure is far lower.
No — it varies; 'a quarter to a third' is the usual estimate.

questions.prompt: Why is muscle loss especially concerning in older adults?
options: They're already losing muscle with age (sarcopenia) and need it for strength, balance and metabolism
Older adults can't take the drugs
It makes the drug stop working
feedback: Correct — added muscle loss compounds age-related sarcopenia and raises fall/frailty risk.
No — many older adults do take them; the concern is muscle preservation.
No — muscle remains essential lifelong.
No — muscle loss doesn't change the drug's appetite effect.

questions.prompt: Someone loses weight on a GLP-1, then stops and regains it as fat. Why is that a problem?
options: They can end up with a worse muscle-to-fat ratio than before they started
It's not a problem — weight is weight
feedback: Correct — muscle lost fast isn't automatically regained; fat often returns preferentially.
No — body composition, not just weight, drives health.
No — regaining fat while short on muscle is metabolically worse.
No — regain tends to favour fat, not muscle.

concepts.title: ★ Saving the Muscle — the newest drugs
concepts.summary: A new class of drugs releases the body's 'muscle brake' so that GLP-1 weight loss is almost all fat. This is 2026's hottest frontier.

cards.h: The muscle brake: myostatin and activin
cards.md:
Your body actively *limits* how much muscle you carry, using two signalling proteins — **myostatin** and **activin** — that dock onto a receptor called **ActRII** on the muscle-cell surface. When they bind, they hold muscle growth back. (Animals bred without myostatin are famously, enormously muscular.)

During rapid weight loss this brake works against you, helping strip muscle away with the fat. The new idea: **block the brake**, and muscle is spared — even built — while the GLP-1 melts fat. Watch the animation: ligand binds → brake ON → muscle wastes; add a blocker → brake OFF → muscle preserved.

The proof arrived in the **BELIEVE trial** (2026): **bimagrumab** — an antibody that blocks the ActRII brake — combined with **semaglutide**. The result was striking: **~93% of the weight lost was fat** (versus ~72% for semaglutide alone), and lean mass barely moved (**−2.6% vs −7.9%**). Bimagrumab *alone* even *added* muscle while cutting fat.

The pipeline is racing: **trevogrumab + garetosmab** (anti-myostatin/anti-activin, the COURAGE trial), **enobosarm** (a muscle-selective agent), and more. The near-future of weight loss may be a **combination**: a GLP-1 to burn fat plus a muscle-preserver to keep the engine. And the cheapest muscle-preservers remain **resistance exercise and adequate protein** — which every trial recommends alongside the drugs.

questions.prompt: How does a drug like bimagrumab preserve muscle during weight loss?
options: It blocks the ActRII 'muscle brake', so myostatin/activin can't hold muscle back
It adds sugar to feed muscle
feedback: Correct — blocking activin/myostatin at ActRII releases the brake on muscle.
No — it works via the activin/myostatin pathway, not by feeding muscle sugar.
No — it's paired WITH a GLP-1, not a replacement.
No — it targets muscle signalling, not fat freezing.

questions.prompt: In the BELIEVE trial, what fraction of the weight lost on bimagrumab + semaglutide was fat?
options: Almost none — it was mostly muscle
feedback: Correct — ~92.8% fat, versus ~72% for semaglutide alone.
No — it was much higher; the point was fat-selective loss.
No — that's far too low.
No — the combo PRESERVED muscle; the loss was mostly fat.

questions.prompt: What are the cheapest, always-recommended muscle preservers alongside these drugs?
options: Resistance exercise and adequate protein intake
feedback: Correct — strength training plus protein are the foundation every trial advises.
No — more GLP-1 doesn't preserve muscle.
No — inactivity accelerates muscle loss.
No — under-eating protein worsens muscle loss.

concepts.title: The Serious Side Effects — the honest version
concepts.summary: Beyond the common nausea, a handful of genuinely serious risks deserve real understanding — not fine print.

cards.h: The gut risks that can turn serious
cards.md:
The everyday side effects — nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation — come from the slowed stomach and usually ease with **slow dose titration**. But a few gut problems are serious:

- **Severe gastroparesis** — the stomach nearly stops emptying; persistent vomiting.
- **Ileus** — the bowel stops moving (a blockage); the FDA added this warning in 2023.
- **Aspiration under anesthesia** — because the stomach empties slowly, food can remain for hours; during surgery that raises the risk of **inhaling stomach contents**. Anesthesia guidelines now advise **pausing the drug before procedures** — always tell your surgeon you take one.
- **Pancreatitis** — inflammation of the pancreas; severe belly pain means stop and seek care.
- **Gallstones** and **acute kidney injury** (from dehydration if vomiting/diarrhea is bad).

cards.h: The rarer but scarier ones — and the honest caveats
cards.md:
- **Sudden vision loss (NAION)** — *non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy*, a stroke of the optic nerve causing sudden, usually permanent loss of vision in one eye. Studies (2024) found a **4–7× higher risk** with semaglutide; it's **rare** (~1 in 10,000), and regulators are updating labels.
- **Worsening diabetic retinopathy** — rapid sugar-lowering can transiently worsen existing eye disease.
- **Thyroid C-cell tumors** — rodents developed these; there's a **boxed warning**, and the drugs are **not for people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2**.
- **Muscle loss** (earlier lesson) and **weight regain** — stopping usually brings back ~two-thirds of the weight, so treatment is often long-term.
- **Pregnancy** — avoid; restored fertility has caused surprise pregnancies ('Ozempic babies').

*This is education, not medical advice. These are decisions for you and your clinician — but you deserve the real list, not 'may cause side effects.'*

questions.prompt: Why should you tell your surgeon or anesthesiologist that you take a GLP-1 drug?
options: Slowed stomach emptying can leave food in the stomach, raising the risk of aspiration under anesthesia
It must be increased before surgery
It makes you immune to painkillers
feedback: Correct — retained gastric contents raise aspiration risk; guidelines advise pausing it before procedures.
No — the issue is a full stomach, not a chemical reaction with anesthetics.
No — it's typically PAUSED, not increased.
No — it doesn't block painkillers.

questions.prompt: NAION, a serious rare risk, is best described as:
options: A stroke of the optic nerve causing sudden, usually permanent vision loss in one eye
feedback: Correct — it's an ischemic optic-nerve injury; rare (~1/10,000) but often permanent.
No — NAION vision loss is usually permanent, not transient blur.
No — it affects the optic nerve, not the skin.
No — that's hypoglycemia, a different risk.

questions.prompt: Who should NOT take these drugs because of the thyroid boxed warning?
options: People with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2
People who have had the flu
feedback: Correct — that's the specific contraindication from the C-cell tumor signal.
No — age alone isn't the contraindication.
No — exercise is encouraged.
No — prior flu is irrelevant.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to weight after stopping a GLP-1 drug?
options: About two-thirds of the lost weight tends to return, so treatment is often long-term
feedback: Correct — most regain a large share, which is why these are often chronic therapies.
No — regain is common without continued treatment or strong lifestyle change.
No — the appetite effect fades when the drug stops.
No — appetite and weight typically rebound.

preface.hook: Your gut already makes something that tells your brain you have had enough. These drugs make it last hours instead of minutes.
body: When food arrives in your intestine, it releases a hormone that does several things at once: tells the pancreas to release insulin, slows the stomach emptying, and signals the brain that you are full.
It is beautifully effective and it is gone within minutes — the body breaks it down almost immediately. That is fine for a normal meal, but it means the signal cannot be stretched out.
These medicines are copies of that hormone, redesigned so the body cannot break them down quickly. The same message, arriving continuously for a week instead of a few minutes after eating.

The result is that people feel full sooner, stay full longer, and think about food much less. That last part surprises people most — many describe the constant background chatter about food simply going quiet.

They started as diabetes drugs, because of the insulin effect, and the weight loss was noticed afterward. They are not appetite suppressants in the old stimulant sense, and they are not a shortcut around eating well — they change how strongly the signal to eat arrives.

aha.title: The drug is a copy, not an invention
aha.text: It is a modified version of something everyone already makes. That is why it slots into an existing system rather than overriding one — and part of why the side effects are mostly digestive.

aha.title: Food noise is a real thing
aha.text: Before these drugs, the constant mental pull toward food was largely treated as weak willpower. People on them report it fading, which is strong evidence it was a biological signal all along rather than a character flaw.

aha.title: Some of what is lost is muscle
aha.text: Rapid weight loss of any kind takes muscle along with fat. That is why protein and resistance exercise are not optional extras alongside these drugs — muscle is hard to get back, especially later in life.

preface.closer: Not a new signal. An old one, held open.
